Net sales climbed  11.6% to $69.15 billion for the 12 weeks ended May 10, net income reached $2.19 billion, diluted earnings came in at $4.93 a share, comparable sales grew 9.8%, and paid household members hit 82.9 million. Adjusted comparable sales rose 6.6% once gasoline inflation and foreign-exchange noise are stripped out.

  Net income of $2.19 billion compares with $1.90 billion a year ago, a 15.2% lift that came in faster than the top line. This move underscores a strategic realignment focusing on capital reallocation toward high-return upstream exploration and low-carbon investments. The divestment reflects ExxonMobil's intent to streamline its downstream retail footprint in Asia, while maintaining Singapore as a key hub for refining and chemicals operations.

 The Singapore retail fuel station sale is part of ExxonMobil's broader effort to optimize its asset base amid an evolving energy landscape characterized by increasing regulatory pressure and market shifts toward sustainability. By divesting lower-margin downstream retail assets, ExxonMobil can redirect capital to more lucrative upstream projects and emerging low-carbon technologies, such as carbon capture and storage (CCS), hydrogen, and biofuels.

Basic earnings per share were US$3.72 and net income was US$15.4b, supported by US$110.5b of revenue. That result appears to confirm the bullish view for now. However, the main story is how sentiment is focusing on that profit figure and largely overlooking what it implies for valuation and future expectations.

Cash flow and debt reduction point to firm capital discipline, yet the earnings step up relies heavily on refining uplift rather than clear volume milestones in Permian and Guyana.

Upstream earnings fell to $7.3 Bn from $9.2 Bn in the second quarter, reflecting lower prices and an accelerated impact from production entitlements in Guyana.
Energy Products earnings more than doubled to $9.1 Bn from $4.1 Bn, supported by higher margins and stronger operational performance.
